lead: Push a wooden block under water and it springs back up. The fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid the block pushes aside. That upward force is buoyancy. It keeps ships, boats and floating covers above water. This chapter finds that force, sets the condition for floating, and measures stability with metacentric height. Stability asks a second question: after a small tilt, does the body return upright or capsize?
prereq: You need: density and specific weight, pressure variation with depth, and hydrostatic forces on surfaces.

blocks.text: Archimedes principle: a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid receives an upward force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces. The pressure on the lower face of a submerged body is larger than on the upper face, so the pressure forces add to an upward resultant.

blocks.where: F<sub>b</sub> is the upward buoyant force in N; ρ is fluid density in kg/m³; g is gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s²; V is displaced volume in m³.

blocks.text: A floating body is in vertical equilibrium when its weight equals buoyancy: W = m g = ρ g V, so V = m/ρ. Here m is body mass in kg and V is the volume below the waterline, not the whole volume of the body.

Draft d is the depth of the lowest point below the waterline. For a body with vertical sides and waterplane area A<sub>w</sub>, V = A<sub>w</sub> d, so d = V/A<sub>w</sub>. Center of buoyancy B is the centroid of displaced volume. For a rectangular box of draft d, KB = d/2, where KB is height of B above the bottom.

Tilt a floating body by a small angle θ. The displaced volume keeps the same size but changes shape, so B moves sideways. Draw a vertical line through the new B. It cuts the body's original centreline at M, the metacenter. For small θ, M stays fixed.

The distance BM follows BM = I/V. I is the second moment of waterplane area about the axis of tilt, in m⁴; V is displaced volume in m³; BM is in m. For a rectangle of length L and width b, tilting about the long axis, I = L b³/12. The width b is across the tilt, not the length.
BM = I / V,   GM = BM − (KG − KB)
blocks.where: I is second moment of waterplane area about the tilt axis in m⁴; V is displaced volume in m³; KG and KB are heights of G and B above the bottom in m; GM is metacentric height in m.

blocks.text: Measure heights from the bottom: KB to B, KG to centre of gravity G. Then BG = KG − KB. The metacentric height is GM = BM − BG = BM − (KG − KB). If G is below B, BG is negative and GM is larger.
Stability rule for small tilts: GM > 0 stable, body returns; GM = 0 neutral; GM < 0 unstable, body heels further. A positive GM means G is below M. This rule uses small angles only.
One experimental check rocks the body and times small oscillations. The period T = 2π √(k²/(g GM)), where k is radius of gyration about the roll axis. A longer period means smaller GM.
Follow a fixed order. Use displaced volume everywhere; never the full volume of the body. Keep kg, m and s consistent.

items: Find displaced volume V = m/ρ from the floating condition.
Find draft d = V/A<sub>w</sub> and KB, the centroid height of the displaced volume.
Read KG from the mass distribution; compute BG = KG − KB.
Find I about the roll axis; compute BM = I/V.
Compute GM = BM − BG. State stable if GM > 0.

blocks.text: A wide, shallow barge has large I and small V, so BM is large. That is why barges and pontoons are stiff. A tall narrow body has small I and large KG, so GM can fall below zero. A GM in metres is read directly as a stability margin.

figure.caption: Weight and buoyancy balance; a small tilt moves the line of buoyancy and fixes the metacenter. For the barge, GM = 2.6667 − 0.75 = 1.9167 m > 0, so it is stable.

spec.title: Floating body stability
spec.aria: Weight and buoyancy act on a floating body; a small tilt gives the metacenter and the sign of GM decides stability.

examples.question: A rectangular barge is 4 m wide and 10 m long. Its mass is 20,000 kg. It floats in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³. Its centre of gravity is 1.0 m above the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the draft, the height of the centre of buoyancy, BM, GM, and state whether it is stable.
steps: Floating: weight = buoyancy, so m g = ρ g V and V = m/ρ = 20,000/1000 = 20 m³.
Waterplane area A<sub>w</sub> = 4 × 10 = 40 m². Draft d = V/A<sub>w</sub> = 20/40 = 0.5 m.
For a box, KB = d/2 = 0.25 m. Given KG = 1.0 m, so BG = KG − KB = 1.0 − 0.25 = 0.75 m.
Tilt is about the long axis, so b = 4 m and L = 10 m. I = L b³/12 = 10 × 4³ /12 = 10 × 64 /12 = 53.3333 m⁴.
examples.answer: Draft 0.5 m, KB 0.25 m, BG 0.75 m, BM 2.6667 m, GM 1.9167 m; the barge is stable.
examples.check:
m = 20000.0
rho = 1000.0
L = 10.0
b = 4.0
KG = 1.0
V = m / rho
Aw = L * b
d = V / Aw
KB = d / 2
BG = KG - KB
I = L * b**3 / 12
BM = I / V
GM = BM - BG
for x in (d, KB, BG, BM, GM):
    print(round(x, 4))

traps: Using the body's full volume in F<sub>b</sub> = ρgV or in BM = I/V. Use only the displaced volume below the waterline.
Reversing BG. With heights from the bottom, BG = KG − KB, and GM = BM − BG. If G is above B, BG is positive.
Taking b as the length in I = L b³/12. b is the width across the tilt axis.
Applying GM to a large heel. GM and the fixed metacenter are small-angle ideas.
Mixing up B and G. B is the centroid of displaced fluid; G is the mass centroid of the body.

quiz.q: State Archimedes principle in one sentence and give the formula.
quiz.a: A body in a fluid feels an upward force equal to the weight of displaced fluid: F<sub>b</sub> = ρgV.

quiz.q: Define metacenter and write BM for a rectangular waterplane about the tilt axis.
quiz.a: M is where the vertical line through the new centre of buoyancy cuts the original centreline after a small tilt. BM = I/V with I = Lb³/12.

quiz.q: Why does a floating body with GM < 0 capsize after a small tilt?
quiz.a: The new buoyancy line lies on the same side as the tilt beyond G, so the couple increases the tilt instead of restoring it. G is above M.

quiz.q: A rectangular waterplane is 3 m long and 2 m wide. Displaced volume is 4 m³. Find BM about the long axis.
A body of mass 5000 kg floats in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). Waterplane area is 10 m², I = 5 m⁴, KG = 0.8 m. Find draft, KB and GM.
quiz.a: V = 5 m³; draft = 0.5 m; KB = 0.25 m; BG = 0.55 m; BM = 1.0 m; GM = 0.45 m > 0, stable.

quiz.q: A fixed mass is moved from the bottom of a barge to the top deck. Which of KB, BM and KG change, and what happens to GM?
quiz.a: KB and BM depend on displaced volume and waterplane, practically unchanged for a small change. KG rises. GM = BM − (KG − KB) falls. A large rise can make GM negative.

quiz.q: Why is a wide flat barge more stable than a tall narrow boat of the same mass and draft?
quiz.a: BM = I/V, and I grows with b³. The wide barge has much larger I for similar V, so larger BM and GM. The tall boat has larger KG, which reduces GM further.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ship designers replace the small-angle GM rule with a righting-lever curve, GZ against heel angle, for large angles and damaged compartments. The inclining experiment measures GM on a completed ship by shifting known weights and reading the heel. Ballast water, free surface in partly filled tanks, and cargo shift are handled as corrections to GM. Search for GZ curve, inclining experiment, free surface correction, and intact stability.
